commenti.body: I didn't have this anticipation at all. I did feel a bit of the bottom drop out once the story shifts into the investigation part, and it didn't quite get back to the heights of the first half which was incredible all the way up until the train sequence. But I think the impact at the end is supposed to come from the emotional devastation, and a sense of empathy and moreso even pity for the intern - it's not that it was a random medical intern who did it, it doesn't matter who this person is, it's that it was someone much poorer than him who was driven by jealousy and desperation. The fact that they were a nobody actually drives this home even further.

I watched High and Low recently with a close friend who'd never seen it before. They had a similar reaction as you to the ending, and were quite upset by the ending. But, Kurosawa was very clearly trying to explore inequality in High and Low, and the ending is a really important part of that exploration. The inequality Kurosawa is exploring in the story is also present in the story structure. We spend so much time at the start focused only on the rich, and their business machinations, only to realize how many people are excluded from this sort of story.

Felt the same way. Definitely felt like the story was constantly trying to lead down a road that would reveal some grand conspiracy or twist. Ending just felt so straightforward and fell flat on me too.

Twists are a kind of cancer on modern genre movies. They've conditioned the viewer to focus on shallow plot mechanics rather than theme. I sometimes find myself caught up in guessing what the twist will be and then the twist on the twist, which is all empty calories. My favorite "twist" now is when there is no twist: the movie is about the condition of the characters and not the self-congratulatory cleverness of a writer's misdirection skills.

I haven't seen High and Low, but it has been on my radar because the Steven Soderbergh-produced Full Circle limited series on MAX is said to be based on it. I thought it was a pretty good show if you're interested in seeing a modern version.

Yes, the POV change to the police and the distance from Gondo in the second half felt like it was building to something, and that extended noir-type cat and mouse chase that Takeuchi was oblivious towards continued to feel like it was moving in a direction that it never led to…
But what if it turns out he was the real kidnapper? And he was actually dead the whole time? And so is everyone else because it's actually purgatory? Crazy right???

Hahaha you’re hilarious. The film has an obvious red herring that wants you to believe that something shady is going on so no, I don’t think my thought process was a grasp at straws. And Takeuchi’s life is in a sense a type of purgatory or hellish torture and the premise of the film is him trying to drag down Gondo from his heaven to Takeuchi’s Hell (hence the alternate translation of Heaven and Hell), so in a sense the anti-twist and actually ending of the movie might be that they are in a metaphorical purgatory?
At least for Takeuchi because he literally IS put into the purgatory state of his cell where he must reflect on his choices before facing certain death
Not a dig specific to you, just a lighthearted jab in agreement with the comment above. Before Sixth Sense no one thought this way.

If you're unfamiliar with Kurosawa's work, you might expect some of the cliche plot devices of more modern crime/detective/mystery dramas.  However, this is not a tactic in which he generally ever deploys.  His films are always precise, clear, and foremost about the humanity of the characters.  By the end of this film, you can't help but feel deep empathy for both Gondo and the kidnapper, and see how greed and classism has shaped the trajectory of their lives.  Which, to me, is something I don't think would be as successful if you're too focused on trying to figure out some clever narrative trick.

A little nugget: High and Low was based on the novel King's Ransom by Ed McBain (pen name of Evan Hunter, which was also a pen name, btw).

Funny you mention Hitchcock. Evan Hunter wrote the script for The Birds.

Source: Evan Hunter was my great uncle.

I think it’s an amazing film, and you can see how it influenced Bon Joon Ho’s films in so many ways (specifically Parasite), such as the way natural elements (water and heat) and verticality are used to symbolize class conditons.

I’d say Parasite is Bon Joon Ho’s High and Low, but in Parasite, the people in the high place never goes down into the heat like Gondo does, and it is the people in the low place that try to move up, so Kurosawa seems to have a somewhat more positive political outlook than Bon Joon Ho does.

Whenever I see a film like this and have this kind of reaction I immediately ask if it’s intentional. And here I think the answer is yes. Kurosawa is familiar with pot boilers and noir. He knows the typical nature of crime stories. But he’s not interested in that heightened reality. He wants to make a film about much sadder, more pathetic reality. The truth is that crime is often not exciting and rarely satisfying. The victims are on both sides. And in this case he is helping us feel the same lack of relief that goes with that territory. 

Kurosawa was often didactic but the things he was didactic about were deeply thought out. So his didacticism isn’t shallow. Here he surprises by the straight forward route the film takes as part of the point he’s making.

the great thing about High and Low working in a genre mode is it's also a great introduction to theatrical spatial filmic visual narrative not just plot devices, akin to Hitchcock but more didactic than titillating. Consider the famously staged blocking of the first Act and it's literal physical geography relative to the antagonist and how this becomes flattened by the end, face to face, interposed through the plexiglass separator. Consider how this kind of poetics can have it's own substance as meaningful as novelistic plot entertainment
